The post WEEKEND READING: Free speech, free labour and emeritus professors appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Paul Greatrix, Director of Higher Education Consultancy, Shakespeare Martineau and Smita Jamdar, Partner and Head of Education, Shakespeare Martineau.

The recent press release by the Office for Students (OfS) trumpeting the launch of its new free speech complaints scheme includes the following statement:

The complaints scheme rules confirm that staff (including academics and applicants to academic posts), visiting speakers and others including emeritus professors, can make a complaint to the OfS where they believe their free speech rights have been infringed.

It is not entirely clear why emeritus professors are picked out as a group that may need particular attention with their free speech complaints, as the reality is that the rules as published actually cover any former member of staff. There is no special status for emeritus professors as listed in those eligible to complain are:

a. a person who is or was a member or member of staff of the registered higher education provider or constituent institution (as the case may be);

As it happens, a subsequent OfS press announcement, on the day of the launch of the new scheme omitted the special mention of emeritus professors. Nevertheless, this did prompt some speculation about what was going on with this very distinct category of former university staff.

Additional provisions for academics

In one area though, academics are a special case. It is important to note there is a specific additional right for academic staff (not others) applying for roles where they feel they have suffered unfairly (presumably by not being appointed) because the institution has failed to uphold its obligations in terms of free speech and academic freedom.

Free speech and academic freedom are fundamental aspects of academic life and, although the rules of the free speech complaints scheme do extend to all staff, there is an expectation that most of the complaints submitted will be from academics.

Given all of this, it is not quite clear why the OfS press release has chosen emeritus professors as the specific category of former staff members to highlight. It might be because there have been several very public complaints in recent years from emeritus professors, supported by campaign groups, about their free speech allegedly being curtailed.

What is an emeritus professor?

The ideas behind the emeritus professor title are positive ones. In general terms, the award of the title is about recognition and supporting the academic to continue to engageme with the institution, particularly in terms of research. The status, though, is usually completely honorary. Unless a specific additional employment contract (which is often precluded by the relevant emeritus appointment regulations) has been negotiated, then the position remains an entirely informal one.

Beyond the recognition of substantial and distinguished service to the university, the award of the emeritus title enables an ongoing relationship regarding research contributions and broader scholarly activity such as PhD supervision and mentoring of junior academic staff.

For someone awarded the title, it is often seen as a recognition of their achievement: an ongoing mark of respect. Over time, for some institutions, this has turned into an expectation for all retiring professors and might even be used as a carrot to encourage early retirement.

There are many different models out there and even more views of what the title should really mean.

57 varieties

There are no hard and fast rules about emeritus professor appointments and every institution approaches the role slightly differently. In many cases there are variations within institutions about how emeritus appointments are made and operate in practice.:

One institution emphasises the honorary nature of the award

Emeritus status is an honorary category of appointment. An Emeritus Professor does not have any employment rights…If a professor continues working part-time…they will not be considered to have retired and therefore will not be eligible for Emeritus status until they retire completely.

For another, the award is automatic subject to time served:

Emeritus status is conferred automatically on all full Professors, Professorial Research Fellows, Professorial Lecturers and Professors in Practice upon full retirement, subject to them having been employed… for a minimum of four years.

Some stress the ceremonial nature of the role:

The Vice-Chancellor shall have power to confer the title of Emeritus Professor upon any Professor of the University on or after his or her retirement so long as the Professor in question does not hold another Office of a similar character. An Emeritus Professor shall, for all purposes of courtesy and on ceremonial occasions, be upon the same footing as other Professors of the University.

Another institution delegates the decision on the award of the title to its HR department following consultation and assuming that various criteria regarding length of service and not being subject to ongoing disciplinary issues have been met. There is also a process for rescinding the title should that be felt to be necessary.

At heart though these are all clearly honorary positions with no legal employment status (unless a separate contract of employment has been agreed which would be precluded in some cases) and no-one should really expect the rights and responsibilities of employees to be associated with the role.

But because of the longevity of the system and the different models there are plenty of examples where things may look a bit different.

Benefits and privileges

Emeritus professors, once appointed, enjoy the prestige of the continuing use of the title and the association with their former employer, something which can feel really valuable if they are continuing with their research. But another part of the package they would be hoping for or expecting would include more tangible benefits such as:

Continued use of an institutional email address and related online provisions;

Use of the Library and related research facilities;

Online journal access and support, including financial, with research publication;

Physical office space in their previous home department;

Laboratory space, technician support and time using major facilities;

And possibly even car parking.

It is perhaps understandable that many are keen to acquire the status of emeritus.

A two-way street

The model works for both parties though as the university also benefits from what is essentially free academic labour from the emeritus professor. By retaining their involvement in the university’s research activities this enables a continuing linkage with any ongoing research projects, grants and collaborations but also previous publications. All of this contributes in greater or lesser ways to supporting the institution’s position in terms of external research assessment and has become more important in the past decades.

The ongoing involvement of the emeritus professor means that they can also continue to supervise PhD students (and possibly undertake a few broader teaching commitments should an emergency arise) as well as sustaining any partnerships or relationships with other institutions where they were involved.

The university undoubtedly benefits from these contributions based on the knowledge that some professors really do not want to leave behind the work which may have defined the largest part of their working lives.

Not all plain sailing

While these remain honorary titles, the risks for institutions are increasing. There have been reports recently of complaints by individuals that titles have been wrongly withheld or terminated because the institution disapproved of things they had said. Disagreements about what resources, services and facilities emeritus professors should be entitled to are not uncommon, especially as institutions tighten their belts and seek to find savings. In other cases, emeritus professors have been accused by current staff and/or students of harassment, creating potential liability for their institutions.

Time to change

No doubt then that free speech and emeritus professor cases will be hitting the OfS this autumn. This really does feel like a bit of a mess though which could do with being cleared up to prevent future distress.

One quite different approach might be for universities to go all in on developing the post-retirement staff community (including through retirement living complexes as can be found on some US campuses) to sustain an ongoing commitment to and from retired academics and professional staff. This seems perhaps a little unlikely in the current climate but does offer a more positive route perhaps than arguments about online journal access and free speech issues. It could indeed be argued that several universities already have something close to this in place.

Perhaps the clearest and cleanest way forward would be for institutions to abandon the practice of awarding the title altogether. Where there is a wish to retain a formal connection with a retiring academic (professor or otherwise) then this should be on the basis of a shared understanding of the obligations and responsibilities of both parties and clarity about facilities provided and payment to be expected for ongoing work. But this would not be an open-ended lifelong commitment and could be concluded or extended with periods of notice as agreed between the parties. While universities may decide that they would still like a title to go alongside these arrangements, at least it will be clearer what the expectations are and when that title and the rights and responsibilities which go with it will no longer apply.

The status of emeritus professor represents a somewhat archaic employment (or rather non-employment) practice in higher education which really does need to be addressed. Removing the title altogether may feel like a step too far for some but clarity on mutual obligations, rights and responsibilities is necessary to avoid future problems.

title: Tunisia’s economic crisis deepens as the promise of a better life fades
summary: Joblessness, failing services and rising costs deepen hardship across the country.
full_text:
Tunis, Tunisia – Like many Tunisian university graduates, Cherine Ghanmi believed a degree would offer her family a way out of poverty.

Growing up in the marginalised town of al-Mazzunah, in the central Sidi Bou Zid governorate, Ghanmi had walked 5km (3.1 miles) to the school her parents struggled to put her through. They hoped she would eventually find a job and support them financially, easing their burden after years of sacrifice.

But more than a decade after graduating in 2012, she remains unemployed. Instead of supporting her parents, she says, she continues to rely on them.

“We studied and graduated believing we had finally found a way out of poverty,” she said. “We thought that once we found jobs, we could make up for all that hardship, repay our parents for their sacrifices and make them happy.”

“Unfortunately, reality was a big shock for us,” she added. “Instead of helping them, we have burdened them even more.”

For Ghanmi and thousands of other unemployed university graduates, the struggle to find work has become a symbol of Tunisia’s wider economic crisis, marked by limited opportunities, mounting financial pressure and growing frustration with successive governments.

The ‘Dignity March’

On September 27, unemployed university graduates began a roughly 300km (186-mile) march from Menzel Bouzaiane in central Tunisia towards the capital, Tunis, to demand jobs and the implementation of legislation intended to provide a clear path to public-sector employment.

Known as the “Dignity March”, it began with 23 participants, according to organisers. More graduates joined along the route, with the coordinating committee later estimating that the number had grown to more than 120.

The journey was physically demanding. Participants paused at points because of exhaustion and injuries before continuing towards the capital.

On October 6, police blocked the group from moving forward in the town of Borj Cedria, south of Tunis. Participants said they were told they could travel individually, but not as a group. The marchers had hoped to reach the Tunis suburb of Carthage, where the presidential palace is located, to press their demands.

For Ghanmi, “the Dignity March was not just a march”, she said, describing it as an expression of the hardship and disappointment experienced by graduates who had spent years searching for work.

Many protesters say they have waited years for promises of public-sector recruitment to translate into real opportunities.

Their demands came amid broader discontent over Tunisia’s economic and political direction.

On October 17, thousands gathered in Tunis to protest against President Kais Saied’s government, deteriorating living conditions and restrictions on freedoms. The demonstration, led by the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), opposition groups and civil society organisations, was among the largest against Saied in years.

Participants voiced frustration over unemployment and the difficulties many households face in meeting their basic needs.

Saied, who has concentrated power since 2021, has presented his political project as a response to corruption and the failures of the established political class. Critics say the concentration of power has weakened democratic checks and balances while doing little to resolve the country’s economic problems.

Stalled promises

The unemployment figures reflect the scale of the challenge. According to Tunisia’s National Institute of Statistics (INS), the overall unemployment rate stood at 14.9 percent in the second quarter of 2026. Among university graduates, it was 26.6 percent. The rate for women graduates was 35.6 percent, compared with 14.2 percent for men. Among those aged 15 to 24, unemployment reached 35.4 percent.

“Almost all the governments that succeeded one another after the [2011] revolution did not make the economic situation, development and the treatment of social issues real priorities,” Cherif Khraifi, spokesperson for the Tunisian Union of Higher Education Graduates, told Al Jazeera.

“Their biggest concern was ensuring they stayed in power.”

Attempts to address graduate unemployment have repeatedly raised expectations. The 2022 Law No. 38 intended to establish an employment pathway for long-term unemployed university graduates, but the law’s implementation stalled amid financial constraints.

Khraifi said measures intended to address the crisis have too often served as “tools for letting off steam” rather than resolving the problem.

The 2025 Law No. 18 provides for the exceptional recruitment of long-term unemployed university graduates into the public sector and civil service. It calls for a digital platform to register eligible applicants and sets out criteria for prioritising candidates. Recruitment is to take place in phases over no more than three years from the law’s publication.

The law was dated 22 December 2025 and published in Tunisia’s Official Gazette on 23 December 2025, when it entered into force. Article 6 provides for recruitment in phases over a period not exceeding three years from the date of publication.

The graduates taking part in the Dignity March have demanded a clear process for implementing the law, including practical arrangements and a timetable for recruitment. For people who have already spent years out of work, another promise offers little reassurance without concrete steps towards employment.

Ghanmi is also sceptical of Saied’s community-based companies programme, which aims to promote local development and employment through projects established by people in their communities.

“The authorities insist on promoting community companies as a solution for jobs and development, yet none of these companies managed to do that,” she said.

Public-sector recruitment alone cannot resolve a problem of this scale, Khraifi argued. Tunisia also needs investment and businesses capable of expanding and hiring. In disadvantaged regions, where employment is scarce and access to capital is limited, starting a business can be difficult.

For graduates such as Ghanmi, the central question is whether government policies will translate into actual jobs.

An economy struggling to create opportunities

Anis Ben Said, a tax adviser and university professor, said Tunisia’s “problem is not a lack of skills, but the economy’s inability to turn skills into production, investment and job opportunities”.

Weak investment has constrained the creation of businesses and jobs, he told Al Jazeera. Poor infrastructure and unreliable public services also make it harder for businesses to operate, particularly in regions already struggling to attract investment.

According to the INS, Tunisia’s economy grew by 2.7 percent in 2025 and by 2.4 percent in the first half of 2026. In September, the World Bank projected growth of 2.3 percent for the full year.

But economic growth does not necessarily create enough jobs for those who need them. For unemployed graduates, the figures offer little reassurance unless growth translates into accessible employment opportunities.

“The financial crisis explains part of the problem, but it does not justify all of it,” Ben Said said.

He pointed to shortcomings in investment and the management and maintenance of public infrastructure as barriers to economic activity.

“Infrastructure investment is not just a public expense, it is a productive economic investment,” he said

This summer, extreme heat coincided with electricity cuts and water shortages in several parts of Tunisia. Disruptions to these basic services affected businesses and added to public frustration.

The Reuters news agency reported that recurring power and water cuts were among the grievances raised at the October 17 demonstration.

For small businesses, interruptions to basic services can mean lost customers and income. Where jobs are already scarce, such disruptions make earning a living even harder.

In L’Aouina, a northern suburb of Tunis, 20-year-old barber Khalil said he was waiting for an opportunity to leave the country by boat.

“There’s nothing worth staying for in this country. Dying at sea would be a relief,” he said.

“I’m going to leave as soon as I can, and let them figure out the solutions on their own. Our generation has borne the brunt of all these crises, and nothing is left for us.”

Others struggle to keep their business afloat.

Khalil’s neighbour, a grocery shop owner who asked not to be named, said persistent problems with the water supply had become exhausting.

“I think the only solution is for someone to take over this shop. I cannot keep up with these crises any more,” he said.

For Ghanmi, the years without work have brought more than financial hardship.

“The wound on the body heals, but the wound in the mind and heart does not heal,” she said. “It really does not heal.”

title: You earn, save & invest. Does that mean you're financially literate?
summary: Financial literacy encompasses understanding one's income, expenses, and the risks associated with investments. Differentiating between saving and investing is crucial for effective financial planning. Individuals must be vigilant against financial fraud and misleading guidance in their investment choices. A well-structured financial plan aids in aligning savings and investments with personal objectives. Familiarity with financial concepts empowers individuals to make thoughtful decisions and manage their finances responsibly.
full_text:
Earning and simply investing money are not enough without understanding how to manage it wisely.

NEW DELHI: "Understand before you invest." Many must have received a message from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) through its awareness initiative, "Samajh Se Investing Simple". But how much do you really need to know about money and investment? This is where financial literacy comes in. And of course, it goes well beyond knowing how to buy shares or start a systematic investment plan (SIP). It involves understanding where your money goes, how borrowing works, what risks investments carry, how inflation affects savings and why taxes matter. Financial literacy is a “combination of financial awareness, knowledge, skills, attitude and behaviour necessary to make sound financial decisions and ultimately achieve individual financial well being,” as defined by the organisation for economic co-operation and development (OECD), an international organisation that works with governments to develop policies for better economic and social outcomes. And as India's investor base expands, an important question emerges: Are more people becoming financially literate, or are they simply gaining easier access to financial products? Or just following the hype and the crowd? According to the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), the mutual fund industry had 28.62 crore folios as of September 30, 2026, while assets under management stood at Rs 82.64 lakh crore. Participation in the stock market has also expanded rapidly. The National Stock Exchange (NSE) reported more than 25 crore registered client accounts as of February 2026, with its unique registered investor base crossing 13 crore in April 2026. Meanwhile, the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) added 3.53 crore investor accounts in FY26, taking its total beyond 25 crore. The shift is also visible in how households allocate their savings. The Economic Survey 2025-26 showed a gradual shift towards equity and investment funds in the composition of household financial assets from FY19 to FY25. The gap between participation and understanding becomes more apparent when investors' knowledge is examined. The Sebi Investor Survey 2025 found that only 36 per cent of investors had high or moderate knowledge of the securities market. The assessment tested respondents' familiarity with stock markets and their understanding of how inflation affects purchasing power. The findings raise an important question: as more Indians enter financial markets, are they equipped to understand the products they buy and the risks they take? So, how financially literate are you? There is no formal set of rules to define it, but here are 10 questions that can help determine it with expert insights.

1. Do you know where your money goes every month?

Financial literacy begins with understanding your income, expenses and savings. Can you identify how much you spend on essentials, discretionary purchases and debt repayments? Do you know how much remains for emergencies and future goals? A budget need not be complicated. Even a monthly record of earnings and expenses can help identify unnecessary spending.

2. Do you understand inflation and compounding?

Suppose you have Rs 1 lakh today. If inflation averages 5 per cent annually, something costing Rs 1 lakh today would cost approximately Rs 1.63 lakh after 10 years. That is why keeping money aside is not always enough. You must also consider whether your savings and investments can preserve purchasing power. Compounding, meanwhile, allows returns to generate further returns over time. But the same principle can work against borrowers when unpaid interest accumulates. Understanding both concepts helps explain why starting early, staying consistent, and managing debt are important. In this regard, Aswini Bajaj, CEO of Leveraged Growth, cautioned against blindly following popular savings formulas. "Understanding the fundamentals is important, but knowing how to apply them to your own life matters just as much. The goal is to make informed financial decisions based on your needs and circumstances, rather than blindly following thumb rules or someone else's advice." Further encouraging people to understand finance better, he added, “Whether you’re earning your first salary, starting to invest or feeling the pressure to match a lifestyle you see on social media, ask yourself: What am I saving or investing for?” He further stressed that the focus should be on using money to achieve personal goals and build financial security, rather than chasing returns or following trends without assessing their suitability.

3. Can you distinguish between saving and investing?

Saving generally involves setting money aside for immediate needs, emergencies or short-term goals. Investing involves committing money to assets with the expectation of generating returns, usually while accepting some degree of risk. As CA Balvinder Singh Oberoi stressed, earning more is not enough; what matters is how well people save and make their money work for them. “Buying and selling shares on any app doesn't make anyone literate,” he said, emphasising that investments must be aligned with financial goals rather than treated as an end in themselves. Oberoi also highlighted the gap between knowing the importance of saving and actually practising it, pointing to lifestyle inflation, the desire for instant gratification and intimidating financial jargon as barriers to financial discipline. Ultimately, financial literacy means understanding your assets and liabilities, knowing when and where to deploy your money, and making financial decisions that support your goals and long-term wealth creation.

4. Do you understand risk before investing?

Every investment carries risks, although their nature and extent differ. Stocks can fluctuate sharply, mutual funds are subject to market risks, and even relatively stable products can carry inflation, liquidity or other risks. Before investing, ask whether you understand the product, its potential losses, charges and suitability for your financial goals. Leveraged Growth CEO Bajaj thus made an important distinction between the ability to bear losses and the emotional willingness to accept them. "Being able to afford risk and being comfortable with it are two different things." Financial literacy means recognising both, rather than selecting investments solely because they promise higher returns.

5. Do you understand how loans and credit cards work?

Borrowing is not necessarily bad financial management. Home loans, education loans and business credit can serve important purposes. However, borrowers should understand interest rates, repayment schedules, processing fees, penalties and the total cost of borrowing. For example, a loan advertised at a relatively low monthly interest rate may be considerably more expensive when expressed as an annual rate. Similarly, paying only the minimum amount due on a credit card does not eliminate the remaining debt. Interest and other applicable charges can continue accumulating. Understanding these obligations helps prevent manageable borrowing from becoming a financial burden.

6. Do you have an emergency fund and adequate insurance?

Financial planning is not just about growing money. It is also about protecting yourself from unexpected expenses. An emergency fund helps cover essential expenses during job loss, medical emergencies or other financial disruptions. A commonly used starting point is three to six months of essential expenses, although the appropriate amount depends on income stability and family responsibilities. Insurance serves a different purpose. Health insurance can reduce the financial impact of medical expenses, while life insurance can provide financial protection to dependants. Understanding what a policy covers, its exclusions, premiums and claim conditions is as important as purchasing it.

7. Do you understand how your income and investments are taxed?

Knowing your salary is one thing. Understanding how much of it is taxable is another. CA Chandni Anandan, tax expert at ClearTax, said basic tax literacy means understanding taxable income, deductions, exemptions, tax deducted at source (TDS) and the differences between the old and new income tax regimes. "Tax literacy does not mean knowing every section of the law. At a basic level, an individual should understand how their income is taxed, what makes up taxable income, which deductions or exemptions may apply to them, and how taxes already deducted through TDS affect their final liability." For investors, it also means knowing that short-term and long-term capital gains may be taxed differently, depending on the asset and applicable rules. Anandan further cautioned against assuming that tax deducted by an employer or bank settles the entire liability. Individuals should also review their Annual Information Statement (AIS), Form 26AS and income tax returns. Simply filing a return, even accurately, does not necessarily demonstrate an understanding of taxation.

8. Can you recognise financial fraud and misleading investment advice?

A message promising unusually high returns with little or no risk should raise questions, not excitement. Financial literacy involves recognising warning signs such as guaranteed returns, pressure to invest immediately, unsolicited stock tips and requests for sensitive banking information. It also means checking whether an investment intermediary is appropriately registered and understanding the product before transferring money. Here, Anooshka Soham Bathwal, CEO and founder of Dhanvesttor, warned that investors can be misled when they focus on a product's apparent benefits without assessing its suitability. She noted that people often follow recommendations from friends, agents or social media without understanding the associated risks, potential returns, costs or tax implications. “People may only pay attention to its benefits in terms of savings and ignore factors related to their suitability and needs,” she said, while shedding light on investors and their tendency to prioritise tax savings over overall financial well-being. Bathwal also highlighted the gender divide when it comes to financial decisions, observing that some women with substantial earnings still leave financial decisions to male relatives or consultants. "Financial independence is not just about earning money; it’s also about having the knowledge and confidence to decide what to do with it." Her advice is to look beyond the promised benefit, understand the product and assess whether it fits one's financial goals and risk capacity before investing.

9. Do you have a financial plan for the future?

Financial goals change with age and circumstances. A first-time employee may prioritise an emergency fund, while someone approaching retirement may focus on income security. The important thing is to identify goals, estimate their costs and select appropriate saving or investment options. Retirement planning also requires understanding how inflation can increase future living expenses and how pension or retirement savings products work. Dr Shunil Tripathi, a financial literacy activist and trainer associated with financial education programmes of the RBI, Sebi, IRDAI and PFRDA,said a financially literate person connects savings and investments to specific goals and time frames rather than following market trends. The objective is not necessarily to maximise returns at every opportunity, but to make financial decisions that support long-term security.

10. Can you make financial decisions independently?

Perhaps the most important test of financial literacy is whether you can explain your financial choices. Do you understand why you hold a particular investment? Can you assess a loan offer without relying entirely on a salesperson? Would you question a financial recommendation that does not match your circumstances? Being financially literate does not mean never seeking professional advice. It means knowing enough to ask relevant questions and evaluate the answers. As financial programme trainer Dr Tripathi further said, "Someone who invests has taken an action. Someone who is financially literate understands why they took it.” It also means recognising that financial decisions should not be entirely outsourced to family members or advisers.

The bigger picture

Financial literacy does not mean knowing every investment scheme, tax provision or market mechanism. It means understanding the basics well enough to make informed decisions, recognise risks and ask the right questions.

What financial literacy means- some thumb rules

Also, the above 10 questions are not a formal test or a set of established rules to measure financial literacy. They are a starting point to help one reflect on their financial habits, identify gaps in understanding and take a more active interest in managing money. You do not have to become a financial expert overnight, nor does being financially literate mean managing everything on your own. The aim is to take an active interest in your finances, understand the decisions being made on your behalf and know when to seek professional advice. Experts can help you navigate complexity, but understanding your money remains your responsibility.

End of Article
